claim: Nanobodies are amino terminal fragments derived from a special class of antibody lacking light chains.
source: Nanobodies, amino terminal fragments derived from a special class of antibody lacking light chains (Hamers-Casterman et al., 1993), are the smallest antibody derivatives that retain full antigen-binding function.
evidence: Supported by citation to Hamers-Casterman et al., 1993

claim: Nanobodies are the smallest antibody derivatives that retain full antigen-binding function.
source: Nanobodies, amino terminal fragments derived from a special class of antibody lacking light chains (Hamers-Casterman et al., 1993), are the smallest antibody derivatives that retain full antigen-binding function.
evidence: Supported by citation to Hamers-Casterman et al., 1993

claim: Nanobodies are composed of a single variable domain of the heavy chain (VHH).
source: Composed of a single variable domain of the heavy chain (VHH), nanobodies boast several features that make them attractive tools for a range of applications.
evidence: Established structural knowledge about nanobodies

claim: Nanobodies have become invaluable as protein crystallization chaperones to resolve high-resolution crystal structures.
source: Due to their compact binding interfaces, they have become invaluable as protein crystallization chaperones to resolve high-resolution crystal structures (Muyldermans, 2013; Steyaert and Kobilka, 2011; Staus et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Muyldermans, 2013; Steyaert and Kobilka, 2011; Staus et al., 2014

claim: Nanobodies have modular serum half-life and superior tissue penetration that are attractive characteristics for the development of therapeutic biologics.
source: Their modular serum half-life and superior tissue penetration are attractive characteristics for the development of therapeutic biologics (Van Audenhove and Gettemans, 2016; Jovčevska and Muyldermans, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Van Audenhove and Gettemans, 2016; Jovčevska and Muyldermans, 2020

claim: Full-length antibodies and bulkier antibody fragments are not normally amenable to intracellular expression, partially owing to the reducing environment of the cytoplasm that prevents the formation of structurally crucial disulfide bonds.
source: Full-length antibodies, as well as bulkier antibody fragments, are not normally amenable to intracellular expression, partially owing to the reducing environment of the cytoplasm that prevents the formation of structurally crucial disulfide bonds.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about antibody structure and cytoplasmic environment

claim: Several groups have detailed intracellular nanobody expression to facilitate live imaging of subcellular factors.
source: Several groups have detailed intracellular nanobody expression to facilitate live imaging of subcellular factors (Traenkle et al., 2015; Maier et al., 2015; Buchfellner et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Traenkle et al., 2015; Maier et al., 2015; Buchfellner et al., 2016

claim: 75 unique nanobody sequences from crystal structures uploaded to the Protein Data Bank (PDB) were cloned into mammalian expression vectors.
source: To this end, 75 unique nanobody sequences from crystal structures uploaded to the Protein Data Bank (PDB) were cloned into mammalian expression vectors, fused C-terminally to a fluorescent protein (FP).
evidence: Describes experimental methodology performed in this study

claim: Many nanobodies degrade and/or aggregate within the cytoplasm and nucleus, while others appear stable and soluble.
source: Transfection and live-cell fluorescence imaging of these nanobody-FP fusions in both 293T and HeLa cells revealed that many nanobodies degrade and/or aggregate within the cytoplasm and nucleus, while others appear stable and soluble (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations and Figure 1A showing representative images

claim: 33 out of 75 nanobody sequences exhibited strong, diffuse fluorescent signal, expected of well-expressed and intracellularly stable and soluble protein.
source: 33 out of 75 sequences exhibited strong, diffuse fluorescent signal, expected of well-expressed and intracellularly stable and soluble protein.
evidence: Quantitative result from experimental observations

claim: 42 out of 75 nanobody sequences exhibited intracellular phenotypes suggestive of intracellular instability, including low or absent fluorescent signal coincident with varying degrees of aggregation.
source: Interestingly, 42 out of 75 sequences exhibited intracellular phenotypes suggestive of intracellular instability, including low or absent fluorescent signal coincident with varying degrees of aggregation (Figure 1A).
evidence: Quantitative result from experimental observations shown in Figure 1A

claim: Nanobodies are composed of three variable loops (CDR1–3) and four framework regions (FR1–4).
source: Nanobodies are composed of three variable loops (CDR1–3), responsible for the majority of target-specific interaction, and four framework regions (FR1–4), forming the conserved framework structure of the nanobody.
evidence: Established structural knowledge about nanobodies

claim: The average CDR3 loop length was 16.4 amino acids for the stable group and 16.9 amino acids for the unstable group.
source: While there was little difference in average CDR3 loop length between the groups (16.4 amino acids for the stable group and 16.9 amino acids for the unstable group), one difference related to CDR3 stood out
evidence: Quantitative result from sequence analysis

claim: 17 out of 75 nanobodies contained a CDR3 cysteine that normally forms a disulfide bond tethering CDR3 to either CDR1 or FR2, and all 17 were in the unstable group.
source: 17/75 nanobodies contained a CDR3 cysteine that normally forms a disulfide bond tethering CDR3 to either CDR1 (first variable loop) or FR2 (second framework region); all 17 were in the unstable group (Figure 2).
evidence: Quantitative result from sequence analysis shown in Figure 2

claim: Disulfides do not form when nanobodies are expressed in the cytoplasm.
source: Because disulfides do not form when nanobodies are expressed in the cytoplasm, this feature may represent a structural liability for intracellular expression.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about the reducing environment of the cytoplasm

claim: Stable and unstable consensus sequences for the framework region were identical except at position 52, where the most common amino acid across stable nanobodies was Phe and across unstable nanobodies was Gly.
source: Stable and unstable consensus sequences for the framework region were identical except at one position, amino acid 52 (IMGT numbering), where the most common amino acid across stable nanobodies was Phe and across unstable nanobodies was Gly.
evidence: Result from sequence analysis comparing stable and unstable nanobodies

claim: Position 52 is one of four hallmark framework positions cited as differentiating VHs and VHHs.
source: Interestingly, position 52 is one of four hallmark framework positions cited as differentiating VHs (heavy chain variable regions of conventional antibodies) and VHHs (Muyldermans, 2013) (heavy chain variable regions of heavy-chain-only antibodies, analogous to nanobody).
evidence: Supported by citation to Muyldermans, 2013

claim: 52Gly has been shown to enhance nanobody solubility, but at the expense of protein yields in E. coli, which may point to decreased stability.
source: 52Gly has been shown to enhance nanobody solubility, but at the expense of protein yields in E. coli, which may point to decreased stability (Davies and Riechmann, 1994; Davies and Riechmann, 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to Davies and Riechmann, 1994; Davies and Riechmann, 1995

claim: 12 framework positions with residues that were significantly enriched in either stable or unstable groups were identified using Fisher's exact test.
source: Applying a Fisher's exact test, 12 framework positions with residues that were significantly enriched in either group were identified, with 4 of those positions having a specifically enriched residue in both groups (Figure 1B).
evidence: Statistical analysis result shown in Figure 1B

claim: 52Gly was strongly enriched in the unstable group (19/23 occurrences in unstable nanobodies).
source: Of note, 52Gly was strongly enriched in the unstable group (19/23 occurrences in unstable nanobodies)
evidence: Quantitative result from statistical analysis

claim: 55Cys was strongly enriched in the unstable group (9/9 occurrences in unstable nanobodies).
source: as well as 55Cys, a cysteine that normally forms a disulfide bond with a CDR3 cysteine in a subset of nanobodies, as noted above (9/9 occurrences in unstable nanobodies).
evidence: Quantitative result from statistical analysis

claim: 54Ser emerged as a strongly enriched unstable residue likely to drive instability (13/14 occurrences in unstable nanobodies).
source: Additionally, 54Ser emerged as a strongly enriched unstable residue likely to drive instability (13/14 occurrences in unstable nanobodies).
evidence: Quantitative result from statistical analysis with inference about functional impact

claim: Position 54 points its functional group into the hydrophobic core of the nanobody, and is usually occupied by a small hydrophobic amino acid (93% of stable nanobodies examined contain 54Ala).
source: Position 54 points its functional group into the hydrophobic core of the nanobody, and is usually occupied by a small hydrophobic amino acid (93% of stable nanobodies examined contain 54Ala).
evidence: Combines structural knowledge with quantitative data from this study

claim: A hydrophilic substitution at position 54 is likely to contribute to destabilization of the hydrophobic core.
source: A hydrophilic substitution at position 54 is likely to contribute to destabilization of the hydrophobic core.
evidence: Inference based on structural knowledge and observed data

claim: Each unstable nanobody had at least one of seven residues that were identified as significantly enriched in the unstable group.
source: Each unstable nanobody had at least one of seven residues that were identified as significantly enriched in the unstable group.
evidence: Result from statistical analysis of sequence data

claim: A threshold of ≥80% positional conservation was applied to generate a partial consensus sequence of the most highly conserved positional residues across stable nanobodies.
source: A threshold of ≥80% positional conservation was applied to generate a partial consensus sequence of the most highly conserved positional residues across stable nanobodies.
evidence: Description of methodology used in this study

claim: Applying conservation-based mutagenesis to all 42 intracellularly unstable nanobodies yielded mutants with a range of between 2 and 12 changes per nanobody, with an average mutational load of 5.7 changes per nanobody.
source: Applying these changes to all 42 intracellularly unstable nanobodies yielded mutants with a range of between 2 and 12 changes per nanobody, with an average mutational load of 5.7 changes per nanobody.
evidence: Quantitative result from mutagenesis approach

claim: 26 out of 42 nanobodies had been effectively stabilized via targeted mutagenesis, as illustrated by strong fluorescent signal and a total absence of punctate aggregates.
source: Fluorescent imaging revealed that 26/42 nanobodies had been effectively stabilized via targeted mutagenesis, as illustrated by strong fluorescent signal and a total absence of punctate aggregates (Figure 7A, C).
evidence: Quantitative result from experimental observations shown in Figure 7A, C

claim: 6 out of 42 nanobodies exhibited improvement compared to their wild-type parent with respect to aggregation levels and soluble protein fraction.
source: Another 6/42 nanobodies exhibited improvement compared to their wild-type parent with respect to aggregation levels and soluble protein fraction.
evidence: Quantitative result from experimental observations

claim: 10 out of 42 nanobodies exhibited no improvement from mutagenesis.
source: 10/42 nanobodies exhibited no improvement from mutagenesis.
evidence: Quantitative result from experimental observations

claim: 13 out of 16 nanobodies that were not effectively stabilized via mutagenesis had 52Gly.
source: Aligning the 42 mutant sequences, grouping sequences that were effectively, partially, or not stabilized via mutagenesis, a striking correlation emerged: 13/16 nanobodies that were not effectively stabilized via mutagenesis had 52Gly (Figure 5).
evidence: Quantitative result from sequence analysis shown in Figure 5

claim: 11 out of 13 additional nanobodies were effectively stabilized after adding up to two additional changes (Gly52Phe and X90Gln).
source: As a result of this additional round of mutagenesis, 11/13 additional nanobodies were effectively stabilized.
evidence: Quantitative result from second round of mutagenesis experiments

claim: In total, 37 out of 42 previously intracellularly unstable nanobodies were rendered stable and soluble.
source: In total, 37/42 previously intracellularly unstable nanobodies were rendered stable and soluble (Figure 7C).
evidence: Quantitative summary result shown in Figure 7C

claim: Ser54Ala was found to be sufficient to stabilize nanobody 3K74 on its own (originally stabilized with eight mutations).
source: After testing several mutation variants for each nanobody, Ser54Ala was found to be sufficient to stabilize 3K74 on its own (originally stabilized with eight mutations).
evidence: Result from systematic mutation testing experiments

claim: Ser53Val stabilized nanobody 1KXT by itself.
source: Ser53Val similarly stabilized 1KXT by itself.
evidence: Result from mutation testing experiments

claim: Nanobodies 3V0A and 4MQS required only Ser54Ala and one additional mutation each to achieve stability (originally stabilized with 11 and 7 mutations, respectively).
source: 3V0A and 4MQS required only Ser54Ala and one additional mutation each to achieve stability (originally stabilized with 11 and 7 mutations, respectively).
evidence: Result from systematic mutation testing experiments

claim: 4WEN was effectively stabilized by 68Tyr alone, when it had originally received five mutations.
source: Surprisingly, 4WEN was effectively stabilized by 68Tyr alone, when it had originally received five mutations (Figure 7D, E).
evidence: Result from mutation testing experiments shown in Figure 7D, E

claim: 1KXQ was effectively stabilized by 68Tyr alone, when it had originally received both Ser68Tyr and Gln80Arg mutations in addition to five others.
source: 1KXQ, which originally received both Ser68Tyr and Gln80Arg mutations in addition to five others, was effectively stabilized by 68Tyr alone, again illustrating the importance of 68Tyr for stability and suggesting only circumstantial importance of 80Arg (data not shown).
evidence: Result from mutation testing experiments

claim: The great majority of interacting residues across nanobody framework regions are located in the most highly variable framework positions, positions omitted from the partial consensus mutagenesis approach.
source: Examination of these interfaces revealed that the great majority of interacting residues across nanobody framework regions are located in the most highly variable framework positions, positions omitted from our partial consensus mutagenesis approach (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Result from analysis of crystal structure data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A

claim: All six mutants stabilized through partial consensus mutagenesis were able to bind target.
source: All six mutants stabilized through partial consensus mutagenesis were able to bind target (Figure 8A and Figure 8—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Result from target binding experiments shown in Figure 8A and Figure 8—figure supplement 1C

claim: 4 out of 6 wild-type nanobodies exhibited increased signal when coexpressed with target.
source: 4/6 wild-type nanobodies exhibited increased signal when coexpressed with target (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: Quantitative result from target binding experiments shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B

claim: Full-consensus mutagenesis resulted in significant reduction of nuclear nanobody signal fraction in the presence of NLS target for 5 out of 6 tested nanobodies, suggestive of a reduction in target binding.
source: Full-consensus mutagenesis, while stabilizing (Figure 8A and Figure 8—figure supplement 1B), resulted in significant reduction of nuclear nanobody signal fraction in the presence of NLS target for 5/6 tested nanobodies, suggestive of a reduction in target binding.
evidence: Quantitative result from target binding experiments shown in Figure 8A and Figure 8—figure supplement 1B

claim: Mutationally stabilized 3V0A-TagBFP showed strong TagBFP signal in cells electroporated in the murine retina, while wild-type 3V0A-TagBFP showed little to no soluble TagBFP signal.
source: Little to no soluble TagBFP signal was observed in cells electroporated with wild-type 3V0A-TagBFP. However, strong TagBFP signal was observed in cells electroporated with partial consensus mutant 3V0A-TagBFP, mirroring observations in cultured cells.
evidence: Result from in vivo retinal electroporation experiments shown in Figure 9

claim: Mutationally stabilized nanobodies are stable in multiple, distinct cell types including rod photoreceptors, bipolar cells, and Mueller glia.
source: These cells included highly specialized sensory neurons (rod photoreceptors), interneurons (bipolar cells), and glia (Mueller glia), suggesting that mutationally stabilized nanobodies are stable in multiple, distinct cell types.
evidence: Inference from experimental observations in retinal electroporation experiments

claim: NBE9 is a nanobody that recognizes an endogenous protein, glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), present in retinal Mueller glial cells.
source: Fortunately, we had in our collection a nanobody, NBE9 (Li et al., 2012), that recognizes an endogenous protein, glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), present in retinal Mueller glial cells.
evidence: Supported by citation to Li et al., 2012

claim: In the rd1 mouse model, rod photoreceptors progressively degenerate starting around postnatal day 8.
source: In the rd1 model, rod photoreceptors progressively degenerate starting around postnatal day 8 (Chang et al., 2007)
evidence: Supported by citation to Chang et al., 2007

claim: GFAP expression is upregulated in Mueller glia in the rd1 mouse model.
source: In the rd1 model, rod photoreceptors progressively degenerate starting around postnatal day 8 (Chang et al., 2007), and GFAP expression is upregulated in Mueller glia (Goel and Dhingra, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Goel and Dhingra, 2012

claim: Wild-type NBE9 signal was almost completely absent within electroporated retinas, with the only signal observed in spherical accumulations in the GCL where it colocalized with accumulated GFAP protein.
source: In keeping with its instability, WT NBE9 signal was almost completely absent within electroporated retinas. The only signal observed was in spherical accumulations in the GCL, where it colocalized with accumulated GFAP protein (Figure 10B).
evidence: Result from in vivo retinal electroporation experiments shown in Figure 10B

claim: A NBE9 variant with the single mutation S54A both rescued expression of the nanobody and resulted in a striking expansion of the signal seen in the spherical accumulations of GFAP within the GCL.
source: A NBE9 variant with the single, strongly stabilizing mutation S54A, both rescued expression of the nanobody and resulted in a striking expansion of the signal seen in the spherical accumulations of GFAP within the GCL (Figure 10C).
evidence: Result from in vivo retinal electroporation experiments shown in Figure 10C

claim: Both wild-type and mutationally stabilized NBE9 appeared to colocalize with GFAP in Mueller glial endfeet.
source: Taken together, both wild-type and mutationally stabilized NBE9 appeared to colocalize with GFAP in Mueller glial endfeet, with variants differing in expression level and, perhaps, propensity to form aggregates with GFAP.
evidence: Inference from experimental observations in retinal electroporation experiments

claim: All five wild-type nanobodies tested in bacteria exhibited hallmarks of instability.
source: All five wild-type nanobodies exhibited hallmarks of instability in bacteria (Figure 11).
evidence: Result from bacterial expression experiments shown in Figure 11

claim: 4 out of 5 wild-type nanobodies exhibited protein aggregation as illustrated by focal inclusion bodies, in addition to diminished cytoplasmic fluorescence in bacteria.
source: 4/5 wild-type nanobodies exhibited protein aggregation as illustrated by focal inclusion bodies, in addition to diminished cytoplasmic fluorescence.
evidence: Result from bacterial expression experiments

claim: All five mutationally stabilized nanobody variants exhibited a marked increase in fluorescence level in bacteria.
source: All five mutationally stabilized nanobody variants exhibited a marked increase in fluorescence level.
evidence: Result from bacterial expression experiments

claim: 1ZV5, 4WEN, and 1RJC mutants showed no signs of protein aggregation in bacteria, in contrast to their wild-type parents.
source: 1ZV5, 4WEN, and 1RJC mutants showed no signs of protein aggregation, in contrast to their wild-type parents.
evidence: Result from bacterial expression experiments

claim: Nanobodies often rely on direct framework engagement for target binding.
source: Nanobodies often rely on direct framework engagement for target binding.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about nanobody binding modes

claim: Positional sequence variability across nanobody frameworks correlates with target interface formation.
source: We show that positional sequence variability across nanobody frameworks correlates with target interface formation
evidence: Result from analysis of crystal structure data

claim: Maintaining framework positions of high sequence variability is important for preserving target binding in some, perhaps many, cases.
source: and that maintaining framework positions of high sequence variability is important for preserving target binding in some, perhaps many, cases.
evidence: Inference from target binding experiments and structural analysis

claim: Nanobody 3G9A has a large CDR3 loop that is normally anchored by an extra disulfide bond to FR2.
source: We were particularly interested to observe target binding for 3G9A, which has a large CDR3 loop that is normally anchored by an extra disulfide bond to FR2, assumed to be lost when translated in the cytoplasm.
evidence: Based on structural knowledge and inference about cytoplasmic conditions

claim: Nanobodies 3K1K and 3K74 normally engage their targets along a concave framework interface, with residues across FR2 forming direct contacts with target.
source: Two of these nanobodies, 3K1K and 3K74, normally engage their targets along a concave framework interface (Figure 8B). Specifically, residues across FR2 form direct contacts with target, representing a common mode of nanobody-target binding (Figure 8B, C).
evidence: Based on crystal structure data shown in Figure 8B, C

claim: Nanobody 5IVN (also known as nanobody BC2) targets a short N-terminal stretch of β-catenin, representing a rare epitope: a short, linear peptide amenable for use as an affinity tag.
source: Nanobody 5IVN (also known as nanobody BC2) targets a short N-terminal stretch of β-catenin, representing a rare epitope: a short, linear peptide amenable for use as an affinity tag.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about 5IVN

claim: 5IVN was found to be unstable when expressed in cells.
source: Corroborating previous findings, we found 5IVN to be unstable when expressed in cells (Traenkle et al., 2015).
evidence: Experimental observation supported by citation to Traenkle et al., 2015

claim: While mutagenesis stabilized 5IVN for cellular expression, it did not facilitate intracellular binding of its epitope.
source: Unfortunately, while our mutagenesis approach stabilized 5IVN for cellular expression, it did not facilitate intracellular binding of its epitope as assessed by lack of co-localization with its target following cellular co-transfection of 5IVO-TagBFP and NLS-mCherry-epitope (data not shown).
evidence: Result from target binding experiments

claim: The lack of binding for 5IVN relates to loss of a crucial extra disulfide bond that normally orients its highly conformationally precise paratope, but that does not form intracellularly.
source: We suspect this lack of binding relates to loss of a crucial extra disulfide bond that normally orients its highly conformationally precise paratope, but that does not form intracellularly.
evidence: Speculation based on structural knowledge and experimental observations

claim: The disulfide bond in 5IVN has previously been shown to be required for target binding.
source: This disulfide bond has previously been shown to be required for target binding (Braun et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Braun et al., 2016

claim: Nanobodies stabilized by the partial consensus-based mutagenesis approach are likely to retain target-binding function in cells.
source: Taken together, these target-binding experiments suggest that nanobodies stabilized by the partial consensus-based mutagenesis approach developed here are likely to retain target-binding function in cells
evidence: Inference from target binding experiments

claim: Certain conformational paratopes may not be amenable for intracellular recapitulation.
source: although certain conformational paratopes may not be amenable for intracellular recapitulation.
evidence: Inference from experimental observations with 5IVN

claim: Conventional antibodies engage their targets in a largely stereotyped fashion, relying heavily on variable loops for target interaction, with minimal direct framework contribution.
source: Conventional antibodies engage their targets in a largely stereotyped fashion, relying heavily on variable loops for target interaction, with minimal direct framework contribution.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about conventional antibody binding

claim: Nanobodies exhibit a greater paratope diversity than conventional antibodies, and contribution of framework residues to binding is more common.
source: In contrast, nanobodies exhibit a greater paratope diversity, and contribution of framework residues to binding is more common (Mitchell and Colwell, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mitchell and Colwell, 2018

claim: Mutating nanobodies to adhere to the partial consensus framework likely minimizes impact on target binding, compared to strategies that rely on grafting variable loops onto established nanobody frameworks.
source: While the possibility that mutation of non-interacting residues will generate conformational changes that impact target binding cannot be ruled out, this finding suggests that mutating nanobodies to adhere to our partial consensus framework likely minimizes impact on target binding, compared to strategies that rely on grafting variable loops onto established nanobody frameworks (Saerens et al., 2005).
evidence: Inference from structural analysis with citation to Saerens et al., 2005

claim: Pluckthun and colleagues were the first to investigate stability and solubility differences between the consensus sequences of distinct families of human immunoglobulin variable domains in non-reducing in vitro conditions.
source: Consensus-based stabilization has been applied to antibody fragments in the past; Pluckthun and colleagues were the first to investigate stability and solubility differences between the consensus sequences of distinct families of human immunoglobulin variable domains in non-reducing in vitro conditions, as well as differences in expression in non-reducing bacterial periplasm (Knappik et al., 2000; Ewert et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Knappik et al., 2000; Ewert et al., 2003

claim: Steipe and Wirtz applied consensus framework mutagenesis to VL and VH domains to enhance intracellular stability for conventional FV fragments.
source: Steipe and Wirtz applied consensus framework mutagenesis to VL and VH domains to enhance intracellular stability for conventional FV fragments (Ohage et al., 1999; Wirtz and Steipe, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ohage et al., 1999; Wirtz and Steipe, 1999

claim: Conventional antibodies are amenable for loop grafting onto full donor frameworks due to their near exclusive reliance on CDRs for binding.
source: This approach was successful as conventional antibodies are amenable for loop grafting onto full donor frameworks due to their near exclusive reliance on CDRs for binding.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about conventional antibody binding

claim: Some nanobodies were able to effectively bind their targets despite their observed instability when target is absent.
source: While investigating intracellular target binding, we noted that some nanobodies were able to effectively bind their targets despite their observed instability when target is absent.
evidence: Observation from target binding experiments

claim: The presence of E. coli dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) had a largely stabilizing effect on nanobodies 3K74 and 4I13.
source: Two of these nanobodies, 3K74 and 4I13, exhibited robust target binding in both their wild-type and mutationally stabilized forms. This suggested that the presence of their target, E. coli dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR), had a largely stabilizing effect.
evidence: Inference from experimental observations

claim: The laboratory has previously described nanobody conditional stability in an engineered context.
source: Our laboratory has previously described nanobody conditional stability in an engineered context (Tang et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citation to Tang et al., 2016

claim: It is expected for a subset of nanobodies to exhibit target-dependent stability naturally.
source: and it is expected for a subset of nanobodies to exhibit this target-dependent stability naturally.
evidence: Inference based on previous observations
